questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: In a cohort study, the incidence of lung cancer is 40 per 1000 in smokers and 8 per 1000 in non-smokers. The relative risk is:
questions.concept: Relative risk is the incidence in the exposed divided by the incidence in the unexposed, so 40 divided by 8 gives 5, meaning smokers have five times the risk; the attributable risk of 32 per 1000 gives the excess burden.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Using the same figures, the attributable risk percentage among smokers is approximately:
questions.concept: Attributable risk percentage is the excess risk divided by the risk in the exposed, so 32 divided by 40 gives 80 percent, meaning four-fifths of the disease in smokers is attributable to smoking.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Which measure of association is obtained from a case-control study?
questions.concept: Because subjects are selected on outcome, incidence cannot be measured, so exposure odds are compared; the odds ratio approximates the relative risk when the disease is rare.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Cases of a disease are recruited from a specialist hospital while controls come from the general community. Which bias is most likely?
questions.concept: Hospital cases differ systematically from community cases in severity, comorbidity and referral pattern, which distorts the exposure distribution independently of any true association.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: In a case-control study of birth defects, mothers of affected infants remember drug exposure more completely than mothers of healthy infants. This is:
options: Recall bias, a form of information bias
questions.concept: Differential accuracy of recall between groups biases the exposure estimate, and it is reduced by using records rather than memory, by blinding interviewers and by using diseased controls.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: A study finds coffee drinking associated with lung cancer, but coffee drinkers smoke more. Smoking here is acting as:
options: A confounder, being associated with the exposure and an independent risk factor for the outcome
A mediator on the causal pathway
questions.concept: Confounding is controlled at design by randomisation, matching or restriction, and at analysis by stratification or multivariable adjustment; a variable on the causal pathway would be a mediator and should not be adjusted for.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: Which of Bradford Hill's considerations for causation is generally regarded as the most compelling when present?
options: Temporality, since the exposure must precede the outcome
questions.concept: Temporality is the only criterion that is strictly necessary; the others, including dose-response gradient, consistency and reversibility, strengthen the argument but none alone establishes causation.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Association & causation, bias, confounding, measures of risk
questions.stem: A screening study reports that a drug halves relative risk, and the number needed to treat is 250. Which conclusion follows?
options: The absolute risk reduction is small, so the relative measure exaggerates the clinical impact
The drug is highly effective clinically
The baseline risk must be high
The result must be statistically insignificant
questions.concept: Number needed to treat is the reciprocal of absolute risk reduction, so 250 corresponds to an absolute reduction of 0.4 percent, illustrating why relative measures must always be read alongside absolute ones.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Child health programmes, IMNCI & school health
questions.stem: Which strategy underpins the Integrated Management of Neonatal and Childhood Illness approach?
options: Syndromic assessment, classification and treatment of the sick child by a trained health worker using colour-coded charts
Referral of all sick children to district hospitals
questions.concept: The approach recognises that a sick child often has more than one condition, so a single integrated assessment covering danger signs, cough, diarrhoea, fever, malnutrition and immunisation status improves both case management and coverage.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Child health programmes, IMNCI & school health
questions.stem: Which programme provides facility-based newborn care through special newborn care units at district hospitals?
options: Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram and the newborn care continuum under the National Health Mission
questions.concept: The newborn care continuum links home-based newborn care by ASHAs, newborn care corners at delivery points, newborn stabilisation units and special newborn care units, addressing the largest component of under-five mortality.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Child health programmes, IMNCI & school health
questions.stem: School health services are best justified on which ground?
options: Schools reach a large captive population at an age when health habits form and screenable conditions are prevalent
Schools can replace primary health centres
It reduces the need for immunisation
questions.concept: Screening for vision, hearing, dental and nutritional problems, deworming, iron and folic acid supplementation and health education all use the school as an efficient platform.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Child health programmes, IMNCI & school health
questions.stem: Which four Ds does Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram screen for in children up to 18 years?
options: Defects at birth, deficiencies, diseases and developmental delays including disability
Diabetes, dental caries, deafness and dyslexia
questions.concept: Early identification and free management through district early intervention centres is the design, covering 30 identified conditions across the four categories.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Child health programmes, IMNCI & school health
questions.stem: Under IMNCI, a 3-month-old infant with fast breathing, chest indrawing and a temperature of 38 degrees is classified as:
options: Severe pneumonia or very severe disease, requiring pre-referral antibiotic and urgent referral
Cough or cold, needing no antibiotic
questions.concept: In the young infant group of under 2 months the classification is stricter still, and any severe classification triggers pre-referral treatment because deterioration is rapid.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Child health programmes, IMNCI & school health
questions.stem: Home-based newborn care visits by an ASHA for an institutional delivery are scheduled on which days?
questions.concept: For a home delivery visits begin on day 1, and the schedule targets the days on which neonatal deaths cluster, with weighing, temperature assessment, danger sign recognition and breastfeeding support at each visit.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Child health programmes, IMNCI & school health
questions.stem: Which indicator best reflects the effectiveness of a child health programme in reducing preventable child deaths?
questions.concept: The under-five mortality rate is sensitive to nutrition, immunisation, infection control and access to care, which is why it is a Sustainable Development Goal indicator, and the neonatal component now dominates it in India.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Child health programmes, IMNCI & school health
questions.stem: Why has the neonatal mortality rate become the limiting factor in further reducing infant mortality in India?
options: Deaths from prematurity, intrapartum events and infection in the first 28 days now form the majority of infant deaths, and these need facility-based care rather than community measures alone
questions.concept: Reducing them requires quality intrapartum and newborn care, kangaroo mother care, antenatal steroids and management of sepsis, which is a different and harder task than the diarrhoea and vaccine-preventable deaths already addressed.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Preventive Medicine in Obstetrics, Paediatrics and Geriatrics

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Concepts of health & disease, natural history, levels of prevention
questions.stem: Administering measles vaccine to a susceptible child is an example of:
options: Specific protection, a form of primary prevention
questions.concept: Primary prevention has two arms, health promotion which is non-specific and specific protection which targets a defined agent, and both act before the disease process begins.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Concept of Health and Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Concepts of health & disease, natural history, levels of prevention
questions.stem: Screening a population for cervical cancer and treating precancerous lesions is:
options: Secondary prevention, aimed at early diagnosis and treatment
questions.concept: Secondary prevention acts during the presymptomatic phase of the natural history to halt progression, whereas HPV vaccination for the same disease is primary prevention.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Concept of Health and Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Concepts of health & disease, natural history, levels of prevention
questions.stem: Physiotherapy and vocational retraining after a stroke represent:
options: Tertiary prevention through disability limitation and rehabilitation
questions.concept: Tertiary prevention accepts that disease and its consequences have occurred and works to limit impairment and restore function, and it includes the social and vocational as well as the physical.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Concept of Health and Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Concepts of health & disease, natural history, levels of prevention
questions.stem: A serological survey in a district finds antibody to a virus in 40 percent of the population although only 300 clinical cases were notified. Which epidemiological concept does this illustrate, and what does it imply for control?
options: The iceberg phenomenon, implying that control based only on notified cases will fail
Herd immunity, implying no further action is needed
Lead-time bias, implying the survey is invalid
Secular trend, implying a long-term decline
questions.concept: Subclinical infections, carriers and undiagnosed cases greatly outnumber the clinical cases that come to notice, which is why serological surveys and surveillance rather than case counts alone guide policy.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Concept of Health and Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Concepts of health & disease, natural history, levels of prevention
questions.stem: Which concept describes the ability of a healthcare system to prevent disease when an agent, host and environment are all present?
options: Modification of any one arm of the epidemiological triad interrupts the process
Elimination of the agent alone is sufficient
The host must be treated first
Environment is irrelevant once the agent is present
questions.concept: Because the three interact, control can act on the agent by treatment or disinfection, on the host by immunisation or nutrition, or on the environment by sanitation and vector control, and combining them is usually most effective.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Concept of Health and Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Concepts of health & disease, natural history, levels of prevention
questions.stem: Positive health, as distinct from the absence of disease, is best expressed by which concept?
options: A spectrum from optimum wellbeing through to death, with health as a dynamic state rather than a dichotomy
questions.concept: This continuum underlies the WHO definition including social wellbeing and the later addition of spiritual dimensions, and it is why quality-of-life measures supplement mortality and morbidity indicators.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Concept of Health and Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Concepts of health & disease, natural history, levels of prevention
questions.stem: Which stage of the natural history of disease is targeted by chemoprophylaxis of contacts?
options: The stage of susceptibility or early presymptomatic disease before clinical manifestation
questions.concept: Tuberculosis preventive treatment of a household contact and antimalarial chemoprophylaxis for a traveller both act before clinical disease appears, straddling primary and secondary prevention.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Concept of Health and Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Concepts of health & disease, natural history, levels of prevention
questions.stem: Why is the concept of a lead time important when a screening programme reports improved survival?
options: Earlier diagnosis lengthens measured survival from diagnosis to death even if death occurs at the same moment, so mortality rather than survival must be the outcome measure
It reflects the sensitivity of the test
questions.concept: Together with length-time bias and overdiagnosis, lead time explains why only a randomised comparison of disease-specific mortality can establish that a screening programme works.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Concept of Health and Disease

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Diarrhoeal disease, enteric fever, hepatitis & helminths
questions.stem: Which intervention has the greatest impact on reducing diarrhoeal mortality in children at a population level?
options: Oral rehydration therapy with zinc, safe water and sanitation, and exclusive breastfeeding
questions.concept: Rotavirus vaccination now adds to this package, and the combination addresses transmission, susceptibility and case fatality simultaneously.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Diarrhoeal disease, enteric fever, hepatitis & helminths
questions.stem: Under the National Deworming Day programme, albendazole is given to which age group and at what interval?
options: Children and adolescents aged 1 to 19 years, twice yearly in high-prevalence areas
questions.concept: Mass drug administration through schools and Anganwadi centres reduces worm burden, anaemia and school absenteeism, and does not require individual stool testing.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Diarrhoeal disease, enteric fever, hepatitis & helminths
questions.stem: Which hepatitis viruses are transmitted by the faecal-oral route and cause water-borne epidemics?
questions.concept: Both are prevented by safe water, sanitation and food hygiene, neither causes chronic infection, and hepatitis E is notable for high mortality in pregnancy.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Diarrhoeal disease, enteric fever, hepatitis & helminths
questions.stem: Which sanitation approach underlies the Swachh Bharat Mission's impact on diarrhoeal disease?
options: Elimination of open defaecation with community-led total sanitation and behaviour change
questions.concept: Interrupting the faecal-oral route at source addresses the whole family of enteric infections including cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A and E and soil-transmitted helminths, which no single vaccine can do.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Diarrhoeal disease, enteric fever, hepatitis & helminths
questions.stem: Which case definition is used for the epidemiological surveillance of cholera during an outbreak?
options: Acute watery diarrhoea with severe dehydration or death in a person aged 5 years or more, with laboratory confirmation in a proportion of cases
Any loose stool in any age group
questions.concept: Case definitions are deliberately simple so that they can be applied without laboratory support at the point of care, with confirmation of a sample of cases establishing the aetiology.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Diarrhoeal disease, enteric fever, hepatitis & helminths
questions.stem: Typhoid conjugate vaccine differs from the older vaccines in that it:
options: Can be given from 6 months of age, gives longer protection and confers herd effect
questions.concept: Conjugation of the Vi polysaccharide to a carrier protein makes it immunogenic in infants and generates memory, which is why WHO recommends its introduction in high-burden settings.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Diarrhoeal disease, enteric fever, hepatitis & helminths
questions.stem: Which measure best controls the spread of hepatitis A in a residential institution during an outbreak?
options: Hand hygiene, safe water and food handling, with vaccination or immunoglobulin for contacts
questions.concept: Faecal shedding is greatest before jaundice appears, so by the time cases are recognised transmission has already occurred, making environmental measures and post-exposure immunisation the priority.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Diarrhoeal disease, enteric fever, hepatitis & helminths
questions.stem: Why does improving water quality alone often fail to reduce diarrhoeal disease as much as expected?
options: Transmission also occurs through food, hands, flies and soil, so a single barrier leaves other routes intact
questions.concept: The F-diagram of fluids, fields, flies, fingers and food shows multiple pathways, so combining safe water with sanitation and hygiene gives far greater benefit than any one element.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Epidemiology of Communicable Diseases

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Environmental health: air, noise, housing, climate
questions.stem: Which indoor air pollutant from biomass cooking fuel is most responsible for the burden of childhood pneumonia and chronic lung disease in rural India?
options: Fine particulate matter of 2.5 micrometres or less
questions.concept: Particles of this size reach the alveoli and cause both acute infection risk and chronic inflammation, which is the rationale for clean cooking fuel programmes such as Pradhan Mantri Ujjwala Yojana.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Environment and Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Environmental health: air, noise, housing, climate
questions.stem: Which pollutant is measured as an indicator of vehicular exhaust and causes methaemoglobinaemia at high exposure?
questions.concept: Nitrogen dioxide is a respiratory irritant that also contributes to photochemical smog, and carbon monoxide from the same source causes tissue hypoxia by binding haemoglobin with high affinity.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Environment and Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Environmental health: air, noise, housing, climate
questions.stem: Continuous exposure above which sound level is generally accepted as causing occupational hearing loss over years?
questions.concept: Risk rises with both level and duration, so halving exposure time permits a 3-decibel higher level, and hearing conservation programmes combine engineering control, personal protection and audiometric surveillance.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Environment and Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Environmental health: air, noise, housing, climate
questions.stem: Which housing standard is recommended to prevent overcrowding, expressed as floor area per person?
options: At least 50 to 100 square feet per person with no more than two persons per room for adults
questions.concept: Overcrowding facilitates droplet-spread infection such as tuberculosis, measles and meningococcal disease, and standards also address ventilation, lighting and separation of the kitchen from the living space.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Environment and Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Environmental health: air, noise, housing, climate
questions.stem: Which measure of ventilation adequacy is used for a living room, and what is the recommended value?
options: Air changes per hour, with 2 to 3 changes recommended for a living room
questions.concept: Ventilation dilutes carbon dioxide, water vapour, odours and pathogens, and requirements rise with occupancy and activity, being much higher for a hospital ward or an operating theatre.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Environment and Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Environmental health: air, noise, housing, climate
questions.stem: Which greenhouse gas contributes most to anthropogenic global warming by total effect?
questions.concept: Methane and the fluorinated gases have far higher warming potential per molecule but far lower atmospheric concentration, so carbon dioxide dominates the total forcing, which is why energy policy is central to mitigation.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Environment and Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Environmental health: air, noise, housing, climate
questions.stem: Which health effect of climate change is most directly mediated by changes in vector distribution?
options: Expansion of dengue and malaria transmission into new altitudes and latitudes
questions.concept: Temperature and rainfall determine vector breeding, survival and biting rate as well as the extrinsic incubation period of the pathogen, so surveillance and vector control must adapt as the climate shifts.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Environment and Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Environmental health: air, noise, housing, climate
questions.stem: Why is the air quality index used for public communication rather than raw pollutant concentrations?
options: It converts multiple pollutants onto a single colour-coded health-risk scale reported against the worst-performing pollutant
It is more accurate than measurement
It replaces the need for monitoring stations
questions.concept: Because the index is driven by whichever pollutant is worst relative to its standard, a good index value does not guarantee that every pollutant is low, which is a common misinterpretation.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Environment and Health

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health care delivery: PHC/CHC, HWC, ASHA & IPHS
questions.stem: Under current norms, one primary health centre serves a population of approximately:
options: 30000 in plains and 20000 in hilly, tribal and difficult areas
questions.concept: A sub-centre or health and wellness centre serves 5000 in plains and 3000 in difficult areas, and a community health centre serves 120000 and 80000 respectively, forming the three-tier rural structure.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Care of the Community

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health care delivery: PHC/CHC, HWC, ASHA & IPHS
questions.stem: Which cadre is the village-level volunteer link between the community and the public health system under the National Health Mission?
questions.concept: The ASHA is selected by and accountable to the community, works on performance-based incentives, and her core functions are mobilisation, escorting for institutional delivery, home-based newborn care and being a depot holder.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Care of the Community

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health care delivery: PHC/CHC, HWC, ASHA & IPHS
questions.stem: A community health centre is expected to be staffed with which minimum specialist complement?
options: Four specialists including a surgeon, physician, obstetrician-gynaecologist and paediatrician, with 30 beds
One medical officer and one nurse
questions.concept: The community health centre functions as the first referral unit, so operating theatre, laboratory, X-ray and blood storage facilities accompany the specialist posts under Indian Public Health Standards.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Care of the Community

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health care delivery: PHC/CHC, HWC, ASHA & IPHS
questions.stem: Health and wellness centres under Ayushman Bharat differ from the earlier sub-centre in that they:
options: Deliver an expanded package of twelve services including non-communicable disease screening, mental health and elderly care, led by a mid-level provider
Provide only maternal and child health
questions.concept: The community health officer, a nurse or Ayurveda practitioner with bridge training, leads the team, shifting the system from selective to comprehensive primary health care.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Care of the Community

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health care delivery: PHC/CHC, HWC, ASHA & IPHS
questions.stem: What is the purpose of the Indian Public Health Standards?
options: To define minimum assured standards of infrastructure, staffing, drugs and services at each level of care for accountability and monitoring
questions.concept: By making the expected inputs explicit, the standards allow gap analysis and provide the basis for facility certification such as the National Quality Assurance Standards.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Care of the Community

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health care delivery: PHC/CHC, HWC, ASHA & IPHS
questions.stem: Which committee recommended the integration of curative and preventive services and the creation of primary health centres, forming the blueprint of India's health system?
questions.concept: The Bhore Committee proposed the three-million and short-term plans with primary health centres and the social physician concept, while Mudaliar reviewed progress, Kartar Singh created the multipurpose worker and Srivastava proposed community health volunteers.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Care of the Community

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health care delivery: PHC/CHC, HWC, ASHA & IPHS
questions.stem: Which principle of primary health care as declared at Alma-Ata is most relevant to the ASHA programme?
options: Community participation, with local people involved in planning and delivering their own health care
questions.concept: The four pillars of the Alma-Ata declaration are equitable distribution, community participation, intersectoral coordination and appropriate technology, and the ASHA embodies the second and fourth of these.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Care of the Community

questions.subject: PSM (Community Medicine)
questions.topic: Health care delivery: PHC/CHC, HWC, ASHA & IPHS
questions.stem: Why does the referral chain frequently fail in practice even when facilities exist at each level?
options: Bypassing of lower levels because of perceived poor quality, absent staff, drug stock-outs and transport barriers
Patients are unaware that hospitals exist
questions.concept: Strengthening confidence in the first level through assured drugs, diagnostics and staff presence is what makes a gatekeeping system work, which is the logic behind health and wellness centres and free diagnostics initiatives.
questions.reference: Park's Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine 27e, Ch. Health Care of the Community
